title: From API to DataFrame: Collecting College Football Scores with Python
text:
Data scientists often work with information that is constantly changing. Sports scores, weather observations, stock prices, and social-media statistics are examples of data that would be inconvenient to download manually every time they change. One common solution is to use an API, or Application Programming Interface.
An API lets one program request information from another service in a structured format. In this tutorial, we will use an ESPN college football scoreboard endpoint to collect game data with Python. We will then turn the returned JSON into a clean pandas DataFrame.
By the end of this tutorial, you will be able to:

send a request to an API with Python;
inspect a JSON response;
navigate nested JSON objects;
extract useful information from each game; and
organize the results into a DataFrame.

The endpoint we will use is:
https://site.api.espn.com/apis/site/v2/sports/football/college-football/scoreboard
This endpoint returns scoreboard information for college football games, including team names, scores, game status, rankings, records, and other details.

Note: This tutorial uses an ESPN site endpoint that is accessible without an API key. Because it is not presented as a formally documented public developer API, its structure could change in the future.

title: From API to DataFrame: Collecting College Football Scores with Python
text:
Step 1: Request the data
Python’s requests library makes it easy to retrieve information from a URL.

import requests
import pandas as pd

url = "https://site.api.espn.com/apis/site/v2/sports/football/college-football/scoreboard"

response = requests.get(url, timeout=10)
response.raise_for_status()

requests.get() sends an HTTP GET request to the URL. The result is stored in response.
The raise_for_status() line is useful because it raises an error if the request fails. For example, a 404 response means a resource was not found, while a 500-level response usually means something went wrong on the server.
We can check the response code directly:

response.status_code

A successful request normally returns:
200

title: From API to DataFrame: Collecting College Football Scores with Python
section: Step 2: Convert the response to JSON
text:
Step 2: Convert the response to JSON
API responses are commonly returned as JSON. JSON stores information using structures similar to Python dictionaries and lists.
We can convert the response into Python objects with .json():

data = response.json()

The top level contains several keys. Instead of printing the entire response, which is very large, we can inspect just the key names:

data.keys()

One of the most important keys is events. Each item in events represents a college football game.

games = data["events"]

print("Number of games:", len(games))

We can inspect the name of the first game:

games[0]["name"]

This is our first example of navigating JSON. games[0] selects the first game, and ["name"] selects its name.

title: From API to DataFrame: Collecting College Football Scores with Python
section: Step 3: Navigate the nested game data
text:
Step 3: Navigate the nested game data
Real API data is often more complicated than a flat spreadsheet. Information may be nested several levels deep.
For each ESPN event, matchup information is stored inside competitions. The teams are then stored inside competitors.

game = games[0]

competition = game["competitions"][0]
teams = competition["competitors"]

Each competitor contains a homeAway value that identifies whether the team is playing at home or away.
We can inspect a few useful fields:

for team in teams:
    print(
        team["team"]["displayName"],
        team["homeAway"],
        team["score"]
    )

Conceptually, the structure looks like this:



JSON field
Meaning




team["team"]["displayName"]
Team name


team["homeAway"]
Whether the team is home or away


team["score"]
Current or final score


game["date"]
Scheduled game date and time


competition["status"]["type"]["description"]
Game status



Understanding this nested structure is one of the most important skills when working with APIs. Before building a DataFrame, you need to determine where the values you care about are located.

title: From API to DataFrame: Collecting College Football Scores with Python
section: Step 4: Extract one row per game
text:
Step 4: Extract one row per game
Our goal is to create a tidy dataset where each row represents one football game.
Because the order of the teams in the JSON should not be treated as meaning “home first” or “away first,” we can use homeAway to identify them explicitly.

game_data = []

for game in games:
    competition = game["competitions"][0]
    competitors = competition["competitors"]

    home = next(
        team for team in competitors
        if team["homeAway"] == "home"
    )

    away = next(
        team for team in competitors
        if team["homeAway"] == "away"
    )

    game_data.append({
        "date": game["date"],
        "away_team": away["team"]["displayName"],
        "home_team": home["team"]["displayName"],
        "away_score": int(away["score"]),
        "home_score": int(home["score"]),
        "status": competition["status"]["type"]["description"]
    })

There are two important ideas here.
First, next() searches through the competitors until it finds the home or away team. This is safer than assuming a particular list position.
Second, the API stores scores as text, so int() converts values such as "31" into the integer 31. Numeric values are easier to analyze later.

title: From API to DataFrame: Collecting College Football Scores with Python
text:
Step 5: Create a pandas DataFrame
Now that game_data is a list of dictionaries, converting it into a DataFrame takes only one line:

df = pd.DataFrame(game_data)

df.head()

The result has a structure similar to this:











date
away_team
home_team
away_score
home_score
status




2026-10-17…
Ohio State Buckeyes
Indiana Hoosiers
0
0
Scheduled


…
…
…
…
…
…



The exact games and scores will change depending on when the code is run. That is one of the advantages of using an API: the program retrieves the available data at request time instead of relying on a manually saved table.
We can also convert the date column into a real pandas datetime:

df["date"] = pd.to_datetime(df["date"])

df.head()

title: From API to DataFrame: Collecting College Football Scores with Python
section: Step 6: Do something with the data
text:
Step 6: Do something with the data
Collecting data is only the beginning. Once the API response has been converted into a DataFrame, normal pandas operations become available.
For example, suppose we only want completed games:

final_games = df[df["status"].str.contains("Final", case=False, na=False)]

final_games.head()

For completed games, we could calculate the margin between the home and away scores:

final_games = final_games.copy()

final_games["home_margin"] = (
    final_games["home_score"] - final_games["away_score"]
)

final_games[
    ["away_team", "home_team", "away_score", "home_score", "home_margin"]
].head()

A positive home_margin means the home team won, while a negative value means the away team won.
This simple example shows why APIs are useful in data science. We started with information designed for a website, extracted only the fields relevant to our question, and transformed them into a dataset ready for analysis.

title: From API to DataFrame: Collecting College Football Scores with Python
text:
What to remember
The basic API workflow used in this tutorial applies far beyond college football:

Send a request to an endpoint.
Check that the request succeeded.
Convert the response from JSON.
Inspect the JSON structure.
Extract the variables you need.
Create a DataFrame.
Analyze or visualize the results.

The most challenging part is often not sending the request. It is understanding the nested JSON structure and deciding how to transform it into tidy data.

title: From API to DataFrame: Collecting College Football Scores with Python
text:
Conclusion
APIs give data scientists a way to collect information directly from online services instead of manually copying values into a spreadsheet. In this tutorial, we used Python to request college football scoreboard data, navigate nested JSON, identify the home and away teams, and create a pandas DataFrame containing team names, scores, dates, and game status.
The same pattern can be adapted to many other types of data.
Try it yourself: modify the code to collect one additional variable from the ESPN response. For example, add each team’s record, ranking, venue, or broadcast network to the DataFrame. Then use that new variable to answer a question about the games.

title: Does Better Quarterback Play Translate to More Wins?
text:
Quarterbacks get a lot of credit when their teams win and a lot of blame when they lose. Passing totals do not always tell the same story, though. A quarterback can pile up yards in a good offense, but he can also pile up yards because his team is behind and has to throw on nearly every play.
I wanted to know how strongly quarterback passing performance is associated with team success in FBS college football. I compared each team’s primary passer with the team’s winning percentage over three seasons. The results suggest that how well a quarterback uses his attempts matters much more than how often he throws.

title: Does Better Quarterback Play Translate to More Wins?
text:
Quarterbacks get a lot of credit when their teams win and a lot of blame when they lose. Passing totals do not always tell the same story, though. A quarterback can pile up yards in a good offense, but he can also pile up yards because his team is behind and has to throw on nearly every play.
I wanted to know how strongly quarterback passing performance is associated with team success in FBS college football. I compared each team’s primary passer with the team’s winning percentage over three seasons. The results suggest that how well a quarterback uses his attempts matters much more than how often he throws.

title: Does Better Quarterback Play Translate to More Wins?
text:
How I collected the data
I collected the data from the authenticated CollegeFootballData API instead of scraping webpages. The API key was stored in a local .env file that Git ignored. The script loaded the key and sent it in the Bearer authorization header, so the credential never appeared in the code, request URLs, or public repository.
The collection process was repeated for 2023, 2024, and 2025. First, the script requested that season’s FBS membership from /teams/fbs. Using a separate list for each year mattered because FBS membership changed during this period. Next, it requested completed regular-season games from /games. Games had to involve an FBS program and have a final score. Conference championship games were identified from the game notes and removed. Games with playoff metadata were also removed, which kept bowls and College Football Playoff games out of the sample. The script was set to stop if it found a tie rather than deciding how to count it after the fact.
Player statistics came from /games/players, requested one week at a time. For each included game, I kept completions, attempts, passing yards, touchdowns, and interceptions. I did not use sacks. CFBD game and team identifiers connected each box score to the correct game result.
Once the game-level data were collected, the script added each passer’s statistics within a team and season. The player with the most attempts became that team’s primary quarterback. He also needed a passing box-score entry in at least 10 included games. Wins and losses came from those same games, so the passing statistics and team record covered the same part of the season.
All rates were calculated from the collected totals rather than copied from the API. That includes completion percentage, yards per attempt, touchdown and interception rates, per-game measures, winning percentage, and NCAA passer efficiency. Using \(Y\) for yards, \(TD\) for touchdowns, \(C\) for completions, \(INT\) for interceptions, and \(A\) for attempts, the rating is
\[
\text{Rating} = \frac{8.4Y + 330TD + 100C - 200INT}{A}.
\]
The script cached API responses in .cache/cfbd. Later runs could reuse a saved response instead of spending API quota on the same request. Timeouts, limited retries, and a short delay between calls also kept the collection process from putting unnecessary traffic on the API. The full script and validation files are in the project repository.

title: Does Better Quarterback Play Translate to More Wins?
text:
The dataset
The final dataset has 312 quarterback team-seasons: 98 from 2023, 107 from 2024, and 107 from 2025. It includes 219 quarterbacks and 136 teams. There are no missing values. The 10-game rule removed 91 team-seasons, and the game filters removed 28 conference championships. The final data contain no ties or sack fields.
The average quarterback completed 62.76% of his passes and gained 7.65 yards per attempt. The average touchdown rate was 5.44%, the average interception rate was 2.40%, and the average NCAA passer rating was 140.15. Teams won 56.89% of their included games on average.

title: Does Better Quarterback Play Translate to More Wins?
text:
Efficiency had the strongest relationship
NCAA passer rating had the largest correlation with winning percentage, with Pearson’s \(r = 0.6695\). Higher ratings usually went with better records, although the points are spread widely enough to show plenty of exceptions.






Figure 1: Each point is a quarterback team-season. Higher NCAA passer ratings generally align with higher team winning percentages; the fitted line summarizes the positive association.



Yards per attempt had a similar relationship with winning, with \(r = 0.6324\). Unlike total yards, this measure accounts for how many throws it took to gain those yards.






Figure 2: Yards per attempt has a clear positive association with team winning percentage across the 312 observations.



The other correlations followed the same pattern:



Passing measure
Pearson correlation with win percentage




NCAA passer rating
0.6695


Yards per attempt
0.6324


Touchdown rate
0.5726


Completion percentage
0.4330


Passing yards
0.3636


Interception rate
-0.3684


Attempts per game
-0.0195



Touchdown rate and completion percentage were positively associated with winning, while interception rate was negatively associated with it. Total passing yards had a smaller correlation than the efficiency measures. Attempts per game was almost unrelated to winning at \(r = -0.0195\). Throwing more often is not automatically a sign of a better offense. It may simply mean that a team spent more time trying to come back from a deficit.






Figure 3: The heatmap shows that passer rating, yards per attempt, and touchdown rate align with winning more strongly than attempts per game.

title: Does Better Quarterback Play Translate to More Wins?
text:
What the correlations cannot show
This analysis does not prove that efficient quarterback play causes teams to win. Defense, schedule strength, coaching, injuries, offensive scheme, and game situation can affect both passing numbers and team records. A good running game can create easier passing opportunities. A poor defense can force an offense to throw from behind.
The 10-game cutoff also leaves out some injury-heavy seasons and quarterback rotations. Choosing one primary quarterback makes team-seasons easier to compare, but it does not describe every team’s situation perfectly.
Over these three seasons, teams with efficient primary quarterbacks generally won more often. Passer rating and yards per attempt had the clearest relationships with winning, while attempts per game had almost none. A useful next step would be to include schedule strength, defense, and game situation and see how much of the relationship remains.
